options.content: A list of characters a computer recognises, each with a unique binary code
options.rationale: Correct: both parts are needed, the list and the unique code.

options.content: The set of keys on a computer keyboard, together with the position of each key
options.rationale: The keyboard layout is not the character set; many characters have no key.

options.content: A collection of fonts used to display text on the screen
options.rationale: Fonts control how characters look, not their codes.

options.content: The number of characters that fit on one line of a page
options.rationale: That is a layout setting, not a character set.

explanation: A character set (such as ASCII or Unicode) lists the characters that can be represented and gives each one a unique binary code.

stem: How many bits does **standard ASCII** use for each character?

options.rationale: 8 bits is extended ASCII (256 codes).
Correct: 7 bits give 128 codes.
16 bits is used by some Unicode encodings.
4 bits give only 16 codes, far too few.

explanation: Standard ASCII is a 7-bit code: $2^7 = 128$ characters. Extended ASCII uses 8 bits for 256 characters.

stem: Why does Unicode use more bits per character than ASCII?

options.content: So that text is stored more securely against hackers
options.rationale: The number of bits has nothing to do with security.

options.content: So that each character is displayed in a larger font
options.rationale: Font size is a display setting, not part of the code.

options.content: So that it can give a unique code to many more characters
options.rationale: Correct: more bits give more codes, for all languages and emojis.

options.content: So that text files are smaller than ASCII files
options.rationale: More bits per character makes files larger, not smaller.

explanation: Each extra bit doubles the number of possible codes. Unicode needs over a million possible codes to cover almost every writing system and emojis.

stem: Which of these **cannot** be represented in standard ASCII?

options.content: The capital letter Q
options.rationale: Upper-case English letters are in ASCII.

options.content: The digit 7
options.rationale: Digits 0-9 are in ASCII.

options.content: A question mark
options.rationale: Common punctuation is in ASCII.

options.content: An emoji
options.rationale: Correct: emojis are only in Unicode.

explanation: Standard ASCII covers English letters, digits, punctuation and control codes only. Emojis and characters from most other scripts need Unicode.

stem: The ASCII code for **A** is 65. What is the ASCII code for **F**?

options.rationale: 71 is G; A is 65, so F (the sixth letter) is 65 + 5.
Correct: F is five letters after A, so 65 + 5 = 70.
6 is F's position in the alphabet, not its code.
102 is the code for lower-case f.

explanation: Letter codes are consecutive: A 65, B 66, C 67, D 68, E 69, **F 70**.

stem: In ASCII the code for **M** is 77. What is the code for lower-case **m**?

options.rationale: Correct: lower-case codes are 32 more than upper-case: 77 + 32 = 109.
78 is the next capital letter, N.
This subtracts 32 instead of adding it.
13 is m's position in the alphabet.

explanation: a − A = 97 − 65 = 32, so every lower-case letter is 32 more than its capital: m = 109.
hints: A is 65 and a is 97. What is the difference?

stem: A program reads the text **"8"** typed by a user. Why must it convert the text before adding 1 to it?

options.content: Text cannot be stored in binary at all
options.rationale: All text is stored in binary, as character codes.

options.content: ASCII cannot represent digits
options.rationale: Digits 0-9 are in ASCII, with codes 48 to 57.

options.content: The number 8 needs Unicode to be stored
options.rationale: Digits are part of ASCII, which Unicode includes.

options.content: The text 8 is stored as the code 56
options.rationale: Correct: digit characters have their own codes starting at 48, so the program holds 56, not 8.

explanation: "0" is 48, so "8" is 56. Adding 1 to the code would give "9", not the number 9; the program must convert the text to an integer first.
hints: Is the character 8 the same as the number 8?

hints: Multiply by the bits per character.

stem: The text **Pay now!** is stored in a Unicode format that uses 16 bits for every character. How many **bytes** does it take?
explanation: "Pay now!" has 8 characters (including the space and !). $8 \times 2 = 16$ bytes.
workedSolution: 1. "Pay now!" has 8 characters (including the space and !). $8 \times 2 = 16$ bytes.
hints: Count the space and the exclamation mark as characters.

stem: The first 128 codes of Unicode are the same as the ASCII codes.
explanation: True. Unicode was designed to be compatible with ASCII, so English text has the same codes in both.

stem: A text file stored in Unicode is usually smaller than the same text stored in ASCII.
explanation: False. Unicode can use more bits per character, so the same text usually takes the same or more space.

stem: Match each character set with the correct description.

right.content: Up to 32 bits per character, almost every language and emojis

explanation: ASCII: 7 bits (128). Extended ASCII: 8 bits (256). Unicode: more bits (up to 32) and a huge range of characters.

stem: Explain how the text **OK** is stored and displayed by a computer that uses ASCII.

points.description: Each character has a unique code in the character set (O = 79, K = 75).
The codes are stored in binary (e.g. 01001111 01001011), one per character, in sequence.
To display the text, the computer looks up each code in the character set and shows the matching character.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Each character is looked up in the ASCII character set: O has code 79 and K has code 75. These codes are stored as binary, 01001111 and 01001011, one after the other. When the text is displayed, each code is matched back to its character.

explanation: Text = sequence of character codes stored in binary; display = look up each code.
hints: Mention the code, the binary and the display step.

stem: A mobile money company in Zimbabwe is choosing between ASCII and Unicode for the text messages it sends to customers. Compare the two character sets and recommend one.

points.description: ASCII uses fewer bits per character (7/8), so messages take less storage / less data to send.
ASCII has only 128/256 characters: English letters, digits, punctuation; no other scripts or emojis.
Unicode uses more bits per character (up to 32), so messages are larger.
Recommendation with reason, e.g. Unicode, because customers' names or messages may need accented letters, other scripts or symbols that ASCII cannot show.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: ASCII uses only 7 or 8 bits per character, so messages are small, but it can only represent English letters, digits and basic symbols. Unicode uses more bits per character, so messages take more space, but it can represent almost any character, including accented letters and other scripts. I recommend Unicode, because the company serves many customers whose names or messages may include characters that ASCII cannot show.

explanation: Compare = similarities/differences on size and range; recommend with a reason linked to the scenario.
hints: Give a point about size and a point about the range of characters for each.

options.content: Standard ASCII
options.rationale: Standard ASCII has 128 characters and no emojis.

options.content: Extended ASCII
options.rationale: Extended ASCII adds symbols and accented letters, not emojis.

options.content: Unicode
options.rationale: Correct: emojis exist only in Unicode.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of using Unicode instead of ASCII.

points.description: Advantage: Unicode can represent far more characters (other languages/scripts, symbols, emojis).
Because it uses more bits per character / has a larger range of unique codes.
Disadvantage: each character takes more bits, so files are larger / need more storage or bandwidth.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Unicode uses more bits per character, so it can give unique codes to the characters of almost every language as well as emojis. However, because each character needs more bits, the same text takes up more storage and more data to send.

stem: A data logger sends the code **01001100 01001111 01010111** in 8-bit ASCII when a water tank is nearly empty. The code for B is 66.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Give the 8-bit ASCII code that would be sent for the letter F.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: The engineer asks whether the logger could send the digit 5 as the binary number 00000101. Explain why this would be wrong if the receiver expects ASCII text.

points.description: In ASCII the character 5 has its own code, 53 (00110101), not 5.
00000101 is the code for a (non-printing) control character, so the receiver would not display 5.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The receiver reads each byte as a character code. The character "5" has code 53 (00110101); code 5 is a control character, so the receiver would not show the digit 5.

hints: Convert each byte to denary, then count on from B = 66.
